layers.name: Bash sandbox (sandbox-exec)
layers.purpose: Sandbox the bash tool's child processes via macOS sandbox-exec. Blocks writes outside allowWrite, blocks reads of denyRead, restricts network to allowedDomains. A host in neither allowedDomains nor deniedDomains asks through the shared ask-tier prompt (ADR-023, ADR-024) — `Allow (default)` / `Deny` / `Allow for this session` / `Allow and remember…`; an unanswered countdown counts as Allow once, Esc denies; prompts are serialized so pi never shows two at once (overlapping selects orphan each other and hang the awaited proxy request), and a two-screen ask holds one queue slot end-to-end (ADR-034). "once" covers the bash command, "remember" writes overrides.allowDomains (applied live, without restarting the proxy); headless denies. `deniedDomains` is a hard deny the prompt cannot override. When filesystem.outsideProject.read gates reads, a pre-flight ask (ADR-015) confirms plainly-named outside reads before the command runs — undetected reads still fall back to the home fence and re-exposed allowRead roots (ADR-014). A refused write is attributed from the error output (EPERM on macOS, EROFS/"read-only file system" on Linux) and offered through the write prompt (ADR-021); a failed write is never offered as a read grant (ADR-022). A path with spaces is kept whole and a bare operation word (`socket`, `display`) is not mistaken for a file (ADR-037). A bwrap mount-setup failure is reported as a sandbox setup problem rather than a write denial, and a write the policy already allows is never offered a grant (ADR-038). Filesystem asks offer once / session / remember only for a path the command itself names (ADR-046): a grant target recovered from output text cannot become a permanent rule, and protected folders (~/.ssh, ~/.gnupg, ~/.aws, ~/.pi, ~/.config, system dirs) are never offered as folder grants. a session grant lives in memory, covers the folder (the exact path when the parent is unsafe to grant) and is cleared at session_start. The blocked path, the deny matches and every grant use the canonical (symlink-resolved) path (ADR-006, ADR-035) — sandbox-runtime silently skips an allowWrite root whose realpath escapes the spelling, so a spelled grant would re-run into the same fence; a `denyWrite` match is a hard deny and a grant that does not take effect is not re-prompted. The filesystem block is rebuilt from a fresh sandbox.json for every command (ADR-033), so a remember from either layer — or a hand edit — applies to the next bash call without a reload; the network section stays live via updateConfig. A second pre-flight enforces the write tier (ADR-045): a denyWrite match is a hard block and an askWrite match asks, before the command runs, using the same shell parsing as the read pre-flight (wrappers, command substitutions, globs, recursive-search folders). The read tier reads a `find` command through `find`'s own grammar (ADR-049): a predicate value (`-name`, `-path`, `-maxdepth`, `-type`) is not a read target, the name and depth filters bound what the command can print, and an `-exec`-family action falls back to the unfiltered walk. A heredoc body is data, never a command, so writing a file that mentions `find .` cannot prompt for a credential. A search command is read through its own operand grammar (ADR-050): after `grep`/`rg`/`ag`/`ack` the first free word is a pattern, so a `ls -a | grep -v` filter whose pattern names `.env` cannot become a read of the file and only a file operand asks; a token carrying regex or code markers contributes only its whole spelling and its quoted parts, so a code string such as `node -e` with `readFileSync('.env')` still asks while a pattern cannot become a path; `rg` and `fd` drop dotfiles from a `.` walk unless `--hidden`/`-u` is passed (they never open them) while `grep -r` keeps them and asks. A committed env template (`.env.example`, `.env.sample`, `.env.template`, `.env.dist`, `.env.tpl`) is read by the guard itself and allowed only when the content scan is clean, so the name alone never asks for a placeholder file and a template that really carries a key still does. Every candidate also carries its exposure — `find`/`ls`/`tree` list a name, `cat`/`grep`/`jq` read the bytes — and a name-only listing of a file inside the project does not prompt, both because a name is not a secret and because the AI can already list its own project; the prompt names the command that triggered it, the exposure, and the `askRead` pattern that matched. Path candidates are normalised with the same resolver Layer 2 uses, so a `~`, `@` or `file://` spelling cannot slip past a rule (ADR-044). A sensitive command fails closed when there is no UI (ADR-017). An inline program that writes a protected path is read by the write pre-flight (ADR-051): `node -e "…writeFileSync('.bashrc', …)"` asks like a redirect, while a read of the same path stays a read, so the guard's own config and extension folder cannot be rewritten without a prompt. The write tier is intentionally wide and the read tier is where the secrets live (ADR-047): allowWrite covers the project, /tmp and the home folder, so a CLI that keeps state in ~/.docker or ~/.composio just works; denyWrite is key material only, and askWrite holds the critical files (.env, .npmrc, credentials, shell startup files, the pi extensions folder) so a credential file never changes under the user without a prompt. An askRead entry may name a folder (~/.aws) and then covers every file beneath it; a conversation grant covers that folder too, so one answer settles the whole store instead of one prompt per file. Only a content read asks: a listing, a walk or a search that merely passes over a credential file learns names and is allowed (ADR-049), and a refusal is remembered for the conversation alongside a grant (ADR-053), so the same file is never asked twice. A client that talks to a daemon socket (docker, podman, nerdctl) has that socket bridged from the host through a user-owned socket (ADR-052): bubblewrap's mandatory --unshare-user drops supplementary groups and denies setgroups, so a root:docker socket is unreachable from inside even though the same user reaches it from a normal shell, and no policy entry can restore it. npm is handed the proxy URL through npm's own config keys because it drops the credential embedded in HTTPS_PROXY and fails an install that curl completes (ADR-054).

tests.expected: PASS=20, FAIL=0 (16 on a host without a sandbox runtime: the wrap block skips)
manual — run with APS_E2E=1 (needs bwrap/socat; initialize can be slow)

knownGaps: Raw-IP egress bypasses domain allowlist (sandbox-runtime matches by hostname only) — XFAIL, accepted v1 risk

The network ask callback receives only host:port, not command identity; an 'Allow once' grant is scoped to the bash invocation in flight and can briefly cover a concurrent user_bash command to the same host

An extension prompt can still be replaced by a pi-internal selector (trust, model picker); the prompt queue serializes only this extension's asks. A displaced selector settles on dispose, so it no longer wedges the queue (ADR-034)
Esc and countdown expiry both surface as `undefined` from pi's select; the TUI custom selector and the select fallback's own timer both record expiry exactly (ADR-031, ADR-039)

Pre-flight ask (ADR-015) path detection is heuristic: the shell is parsed (wrappers, substitutions, globs, recursive-search folders, ADR-045) but a path built at runtime (variable expansion, a compiled helper, a script file) is not prompted

askRead (ADR-019) pre-flight is heuristic too: an obfuscated read of an askRead path is not prompted (put the path in denyRead to hard-deny it). A name-only listing of such a file never asks, inside the project or outside it, and a search pattern is never a path (ADR-049, ADR-050, ADR-053). A refusal is remembered for the rest of the conversation, so the same file is not asked twice; clearing it needs a new conversation

The bash network allowlist is advisory while network.allowLocalhost is true: on Linux that removes --unshare-net, so a client that ignores HTTPS_PROXY reaches any host directly (raw-IP egress has the same effect under the proxy)
The Advanced Secure output gate sees tool output only: a command that reads a secret and sends it out itself never passes through it
Write attribution is post-hoc (ADR-021): the command has already failed when the prompt appears, and a command whose output never names the operand cannot be attributed

Symlink-resolved grants (ADR-035) can still fail if the resolved folder is removed, replaced with a symlink, or is not bindable by the runtime; the per-invocation grant-ineffective guard blocks the prompt loop in that case

Writes are wide by default (ADR-047): a compromised agent can corrupt project files, shell rc files ask rather than block, and only key material is hard-denied. Token protection is on the read side (askRead + the output scan), not on writes.

The daemon socket bridge (ADR-052) hands a sandboxed command the authority the user's group membership carries: anything that reaches the bridged socket can drive the daemon, which for docker is host root. It is started only for the daemon clients (docker, podman, nerdctl, buildah, skopeo) and lives for that one command

A recursive search no longer asks for the askRead files it walks (ADR-053): the walk is a name, so `grep -rn .` over a tree can print what a `.npmrc` holds. The Advanced Secure output gate is what stops those bytes; in Default mode only the pattern stands between the model and the file, so keep credential stores in denyRead when that matters

layers.name: In-process tool guard
layers.purpose: Catch what sandbox-exec can't: the in-process read/grep/find/ls/write/edit/fetch_content/web_search/get_search_content tools. Same policy file as L1. grep output lines from denied files beneath an allowed search root are removed before they reach the model (ADR-008). Denied domains are a hard block, never ask-able (ADR-023); an unknown domain asks with once/session/remember. In Advanced Secure mode (ADR-018) it also flags sensitive filenames and risky MCP tool calls before they run, and redacts detected secrets from any tool output before it reaches the model. The MCP gate ignores the server namespace, classifies from the head verb of the name or description, asks for destructive names/arguments and mutating names, and fails closed only for tools with no description; `sandbox.json` -> `mcp` tunes it (allow/ask lists, annotation trust, threshold) per ADR-032. Ask prompts are keyboard-only (ADR-036): mouse clicks and wheel are inert, so only ↑/↓ moves the highlight and only Enter picks. The countdown ends at the first ↑/↓, so a user who has started choosing is resolved only by Enter/Esc, never by the timer (ADR-039). Path matching normalises the spelled path the way pi's own tools do before resolving it (ADR-044): `~`, `@`, `file://` and folded Unicode spaces reach the same absolute path, so the rule and the file agree. An askRead hit is a one-read prompt with no `always` option and is never persisted (ADR-046), and the grep result filter removes askRead lines as well as denyRead ones. isDeniedWrite consults askWrite as well as denyWrite, so the model's write tool asks for a critical file even when a wide allowWrite root covers it. An explicit filesystem.allowRead (or an overrides.allowRead entry) wins over an askRead folder, which is the escape hatch for a store whose files are not all secret; denyRead still wins over both (ADR-047).
knownGaps: Live end-to-end tests via the actual tools are manual today (no in-session test harness in pi yet)
fetch_content redirects are not re-checked against the allowlist
web_search itself is not domain-checked (only its follow-on fetch_content is)
find and ls still print names (not contents) of denied files beneath an allowed root (ADR-008, accepted)
The grep output filter parses pi's grep line format; a format change leaves lines unfiltered until grep-filter.mjs is updated
Path parity (ADR-044) is an invariant over pi's resolver, not a copy of it: a pi release that changes how it normalises `~`, `@` or `file://` can re-open the bypass until user-path.mjs is updated
A hand-written overrides.allowRead entry still wins over askRead (deliberate: explicit user intent)

MCP gate heuristics read tool names and description heads; a server that only states its operation in prose deeper in the description (or that omits descriptions entirely) may still ask — tune it with the `mcp` policy lists (ADR-032)

askRead entries that name files ask per file; only folder entries and conversation grants collapse a store into one prompt. A vendor folder that is not listed is not asked about — the content scan is the backstop, not a path rule.
A bare askRead/askWrite/denyRead entry matches a file name only; a store needs a path spelling (~/.pi/agent/sessions, not sessions). default-policy.mjs pins the transcript case.

A tool result that carries a data block instead of text (an image, an attachment) cannot be scanned: it is reported as unscannable and asks in Advanced Secure instead of being forwarded, except for the read tool, which returns images on purpose.

A program can still copy a secret it read into a new file or send it out. An inline program (`node -e`, `python -c`) is read by the write pre-flight when it names a write API next to a protected path (ADR-051), but a script file it runs is opaque, and the output gate covers what the model sees, not what the host emits. allowAllUnixSockets, allowLocalhost and allowedDomains are the egress limits, and the first two are relaxed by default on purpose (docker, SSH agent, local dev servers).

Bash children inherit the user's environment, so a token the user exported into pi's shell is visible to echo $VAR. pi's own provider key is not inherited (it is resolved from auth.json, not the environment).

layers.name: Subagent posture
layers.purpose: Stricter network policy when ctx.hasUI === false (subagents, -p mode, JSON mode). Filesystem deny rules apply unchanged in every context.

config.note: research-only uses a transcript heuristic to identify librarian/scout/researcher agents. Best-effort; v2 should plumb agent identity through ctx.

tests.command: echo 'manual: set subagent.network=deny in sandbox.json, run pi -p "fetch https://example.com"; expect block'

knownGaps: ctx.hasUI=false also catches legitimate scripted runs, not just subagents — that's why default is 'allow'
No first-class agent identity in ctx

layers.name: Browser gate (chrome_devtools_*)
layers.purpose: Per-session ctx.ui.confirm for mutating chrome_devtools_* tools (navigate_page, click, fill, evaluate_script, etc.). Read-only ops (snapshot, screenshot) stay open. Subagents always denied.
knownGaps: entire layer not implemented

uxPolish.what: src/l1-sandbox/bash-ops.ts scans merged stdout+stderr for EPERM/EACCES/EROFS/"read-only file system", so `cmd 2>&1 | head` still triggers the hint.

Layer 1 attributes the refused path from errno-style output (`EROFS: read-only file system, open '/path'`, `cannot touch '/path': Read-only file system`) and routes a Linux EROFS write to the write prompt; a failed write is never mistaken for an outside-project read, so it cannot offer a useless read grant (ADR-022).

Hint extracts the offending path and recognizes tool config dirs (~/.config/, ~/.kube/, ~/.docker/, ~/.netrc, ~/.aws/, ~/.npmrc, ~/.gitconfig). Suggests a project-local .pi/sandbox.json snippet with the path pre-filled. Says explicitly 'this is the pi sandbox, NOT macOS TCC' so the model stops misdiagnosing.
Ask-tier UX: when sandbox blocks AND ctx.hasUI, prompt 'Retry without sandbox? [y/N/always-for-this-cwd]'. 'always' writes path into <cwd>/.pi/sandbox.json. Avoids per-command-prompt antipattern.
